posts.post_text: We banned ChatGPT in our analytics department last month. Not because AI is bad — because nobody could explain where the numbers came from. When a regulator asks 'how did you arrive at this figure?' and the answer is 'GPT said so', you've got a compliance problem. The AI trust gap is real and growing.
posts.angle: High-scoring compliance pain post with three ICP prospects engaging — validate the 'explainability' problem as the real blocker, not AI itself, and plant a sharp question about what auditability actually requires
posts.draft_comment: The ban makes complete sense — it's not really an AI problem, it's an audit trail problem. 'The model said so' has never been a defensible answer in a regulated environment, and most of these tools weren't built with that constraint in mind. Curious whether the bar for your team is full methodology transparency or just something a human can actually stand behind when challenged?

posts.post_text: We spent 18 months building a Power BI dashboard that our finance team refuses to use. They still export everything to Excel and email it around. The building part was easy. Getting people to actually trust the numbers enough to quote them in a board meeting? That's the real challenge nobody talks about. Anyone else hit this wall?
posts.angle: ICP prospect COO frustrated with Power BI adoption — validate the real pain (trust, not tooling) and add a sharp insight without pitching
posts.draft_comment: The Excel thing isn't stubbornness — it's a trust problem wearing a workflow costume. Your finance team isn't wrong to be skeptical, they've probably been burned by numbers that looked right until they weren't. The dashboard was never the product. The product was confidence in the number at 9am on board meeting day.

posts.post_text: Unpopular opinion: most operational dashboards are vanity projects. We had 47 KPIs on our ops dashboard. Nobody looked at it. Cut it to 5 metrics that actually drive decisions. Usage went from 10% to 85%. The problem with BI isn't the tools — it's that we measure everything and understand nothing.
posts.angle: ICP prospect (Director of Operations at Summit Group) engaging with a post about dashboard bloat — validate the 47-to-5 insight, add the 'why people stop looking' layer, no pitch
posts.draft_comment: 47 KPIs is actually pretty common — I've seen teams hit 80+. The thing nobody talks about is why usage drops: it's not laziness, it's that people open the dashboard, can't figure out what it's telling them to *do*, and quietly stop opening it. Cutting to 5 forced the real question — what decision does this metric actually serve? Most orgs skip that question entirely and wonder why the tool 'doesn't work.'

posts.post_text: Hot take: self-service BI is a myth. We gave everyone Power BI licenses and what happened? 200 reports, zero consistency, three different definitions of 'revenue'. The promise of democratising data is great until you realise nobody agrees on what the data means. Build vs buy isn't the question — it's 'who owns the truth?'
posts.angle: High-scoring post with ICP prospect (Innovation Director at NorthStar Retail) engaging — validate the 'who owns the truth' framing, add the insight that tooling isn't the problem, governance is, and let the question land on Lisa too
posts.draft_comment: The 200 reports thing is so predictable it's almost a rite of passage. Everyone assumes the bottleneck is access to data — turns out it's agreeing on what the data *means* before anyone touches a dashboard. Tooling doesn't fix that. What did you find actually moves the needle — top-down mandates, or did it have to come from the analysts themselves?

posts.post_text: AI hallucinations in analytics are a security issue, not just an accuracy issue. If your AI tool generates a financial report with hallucinated numbers and someone makes a decision based on it, that's not a bug — it's a material risk. We need to start treating AI outputs with the same scrutiny as we treat user inputs.
posts.angle: CISO raising AI hallucination as a security risk with a CEO prospect engaging — validate the reframing, add the trust layer insight, no pitch
posts.draft_comment: The 'user input scrutiny' framing is exactly right — most teams are running input validation on one side and basically vibes-checking on the other. What's interesting is this isn't even a new problem, it's the old data quality problem wearing a new coat. The difference is the confidence. A bad SQL query looks broken. A hallucinated summary sounds authoritative. Who in your org is actually owning that verification layer right now?

posts.post_text: Had a fascinating conversation with a client yesterday. They spent £200k on a BI platform and the only person who can use it is the one who built it. Self-service my arse. The gap between what vendors promise and what actually happens in a 50-person company is enormous. When will the industry admit that most BI tools are built for data teams, not business teams?
posts.angle: ICP prospect (COO at Sterling Consulting) engaging with BI adoption frustration — validate the core problem with a specific observation, add the 'built for builders not users' insight without pitching
posts.draft_comment: That £200k number is almost beside the point — the real cost is 18 months of people quietly going back to spreadsheets because asking for a report feels like filing a ticket. The 'self-service' label has been doing a lot of heavy lifting for tools that still require someone to know what a dimension is. Most platforms are built so a data person can move fast, not so a COO can get an answer on a Tuesday without chasing anyone. Wondering if anyone's actually cracked that or if we're all just pretending the training will fix it.

posts.post_text: Just had our quarterly review and the CFO asked why the numbers in our BI dashboard don't match the numbers in the ERP. Turns out three different teams were applying different filters to the same dataset. AI won't fix this. Culture will. But nobody wants to hear that.
posts.angle: Commercial Director calling out a data governance/culture problem that's endemic in mid-market — validate the diagnosis, add the layer he's missing about how tooling can either reinforce or undermine that culture change
posts.draft_comment: The filter problem is almost never about filters. It's that three teams had three different questions and nobody agreed on the answer before they started pulling data. Culture has to lead, but I'd push back slightly — the right tooling can either make that culture problem invisible until it explodes in a CFO review, or it can surface the disagreement early enough that someone actually fixes it. How long had those three versions been floating around before the quarterly?

posts.post_text: Rolled out Copilot to 500 users last quarter. Usage after 90 days? 12%. The problem isn't the tool — it's that nobody knows what to ask it. We're essentially paying for a very expensive autocomplete. Shadow AI is the real story here — people are using ChatGPT on their phones because Copilot is too locked down.
posts.angle: IT Director surfacing the real adoption gap behind enterprise AI rollouts — validate the shadow AI observation and add the 'knowing what to ask' insight as a structural problem, not a training one
posts.draft_comment: The 12% number is almost identical to what I keep hearing from people who've done similar rollouts. Shadow AI on personal phones is the tell — it's not that people don't want AI, it's that they want one that meets them where they already have a question, not one that waits for them to figure out the right prompt. That gap between 'tool is available' and 'tool is useful to me specifically' is way harder to close than most rollouts assume. How are you thinking about fixing that — more training, or something structural?
